lede: Sunlight on your face, a radio in the kitchen, a phone finding a signal, an X-ray at the dentist. They are one family of wave stretched to very different lengths, and the family runs in a fixed order.
can: Name the seven regions in order, in either direction
State what all seven share: transverse, and one speed in a vacuum
Give the specification's danger for each region, naming the part of the body

md: Sunlight warming your face, a phone finding a signal, the beep of a microwave oven, a dentist taking an X-ray. Those are all the same kind of wave, stretched to very different lengths. Together they make one family, and the family runs in a fixed order.

md:
Reading left to right the **wavelength gets shorter** and the **frequency gets higher**. Reading right to left, the opposite. That single strip answers most questions on this topic, because nearly all of them ask you to place a region, or to compare two of them.
The order is worth saying out loud until it sticks: **radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays**.

prompt: Which region sits between infrared and ultraviolet?
explain: Visible light — the only part of the whole spectrum your eyes can detect.

text: 2. What all seven have in common

alt: Three electromagnetic waves of very different wavelength drawn between the same two lines, showing that they start together and arrive together because all travel at 3 × 10⁸ metres per second in a vacuum.
caption: Different wavelengths, different frequencies — but they cross the gap together.

md: Two things never change across the whole family. Every region is a **transverse** wave, and in a **vacuum** every region travels at the **same speed**: 3 × 10⁸ m/s. A gamma ray is not faster than a radio wave; it simply fits far more waves into each second.

title: Why the strip is a spectrum and not a list
md: Because the speed is fixed, wavelength and frequency are locked together: if one doubles the other halves. That is what $v = f\lambda$ says when $v$ cannot change. So the seven regions are not seven different things — they are one continuous range, cut into seven named pieces for convenience.

prompt: A radio signal and a gamma ray leave the same star at the same moment. Which reaches the Earth first?
options: the gamma ray, because its frequency is higher
the radio signal, because its wavelength is longer
explain: Together. In a vacuum every electromagnetic wave travels at the same speed, so the same distance takes the same time.

title: One equation, and it is not printed
md: $v = f\lambda$ — and for any electromagnetic wave in a vacuum $v$ is always 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Rearranged: $\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f}$ and $f = \dfrac{v}{\lambda}$. P2 prints no formula sheet: write the equation from memory, and write it first.

caption: The answer, drawn: one complete wave takes up 3 m.

md:
**Worked example.** A radio station broadcasts at 1 × 10⁸ Hz.
**Step 1** — write the equation: $v = f\lambda$.
**Step 2** — rearrange for what you want: $\lambda = v \div f$.
**Step 3** — substitute: $\lambda = 3 \times 10^{8} \div 1 \times 10^{8}$.
**Step 4** — answer with the unit: $\lambda = 3$ m. Radio waves really are metres long, which is why radio aerials are so big.

prompt: A microwave transmitter works at 3 × 10⁹ Hz. Calculate its wavelength, in m.
explain: $\lambda = v \div f = 3 \times 10^{8} \div 3 \times 10^{9} = 0.1$ m. Microwaves are centimetres long, so a wavelength of about a tenth of a metre is believable.

alt: A thermal camera image of a dog. The warmest parts, its eyes, nose and the inside of its ears, appear brightest, while the thick fur over its body appears much darker because less infrared escapes through it.
caption: A thermal camera sees no visible light at all. Everything in this picture is infrared, and the brightest parts are the warmest.
prompt: The nose and the inside of the ears are brightest, the thick fur is darkest. Say what that tells you about which objects emit infrared, and give the danger of too much infrared falling on your skin.

md:
Every region can harm you if you get too much of it, and the specification names one harm for each. **Microwaves** — internal heating of body tissues. **Infrared** — felt as heat, burns the skin. **Ultraviolet** — damages skin cells, which can lead to skin cancer. **Intense visible light** — damages the eyes. **X-rays and gamma rays** — damage cells, which may lead to cancer.
The pattern behind the list: the **higher the frequency, the more damage**.

options: burning the surface of the skin
explain: Internal heating of body tissues. Surface burns belong to infrared and skin-cell damage to ultraviolet; the word internal is what separates the microwave answer from the others.

text: 5. See the whole family at once

title: GCSE Physics Revision "Electromagnetic Waves"
why: Five minutes running the whole spectrum end to end, with the uses and dangers of each region.

prompt: Which two quantities change as you move along the electromagnetic spectrum, and which one does not?
options: wavelength and frequency change; the speed in a vacuum does not
wavelength and speed change; the frequency does not
frequency and speed change; the wavelength does not
answer: wavelength and frequency change; the speed in a vacuum does not
explain: Wavelength and frequency change from region to region; the speed in a vacuum is the same for all seven.

title: Recap — you can now
md:
Name the seven regions in order, in either direction.
Say that all seven are transverse and all travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum.
Use $v = f\lambda$ with the speed of light to find a wavelength or a frequency.
Give the specification's danger for each region, in its own words.
Explain why higher frequency means more damage.

Put the seven regions in order, either way round.
Say what all seven have in common.
Work out a wavelength from the speed of light.
Name a use and a danger for each region, with the body part.

Usually a table to complete, regions in one column and uses or dangers in the other, at a mark each; it has carried the six-mark banded question more than once. A calculation with the speed of light appears at Higher. Read whether the question wants wavelength order or frequency order before you write, and give every danger a body part.
